```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 110)
library(sciparseR)
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "sciparseR")
```

Extraction answers questions such as "what was the design?", "how many
were randomized?" and "what was the hazard ratio for the primary outcome
at 12 months in the intention-to-treat population?". The answer to the
last one is not a number: it is a number *with its context*, and getting
the context wrong (the wrong arm, time point or analysis set) is the most
common and most harmful extraction error. This article shows how
sciparseR represents results so that the context is explicit and
checkable.

## Schemas

A schema is a list of fields. Five schemas are built in:

```{r}
sc_schema("clinical_trial")
```

`sc_extract_pico()`, `sc_extract_methods()`, `sc_extract_outcomes()` and
`sc_extract_statistics()` are shortcuts for the built-in schemas.

## Records

The result of `sc_extract()` has one row per extracted value:

```{r}
doc <- sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf"))
x <- sc_extract(doc, "clinical_trial")
names(x$records)
```

The columns that matter most:

* `field`, `value`, `value_num`, `unit`: what was found. `value` is the
  text exactly as printed; `value_num` its numeric reading.
* `status`: `reported`, `missing` (the source marks it missing, for
  example with a dash), `not_reported` (expected but absent),
  `not_assessed` (absent, but part of the text was never assessed because
  a model answer could not be read), `ambiguous`
  (found, but its meaning is not stated), `unsupported` (model output that
  could not be verified), `superseded` (replaced by a correction).
* `data_origin`: `reported`, `derived`, `model_inferred`,
  `human_corrected`.
* `evidence_id`: the link to the evidence row.
* `interval_type` (`confidence`, `credible`, `prediction`) and `ci_level`
  for interval bounds; `p_operator` (`=`, `<`, `>`, and so on) and
  `test_role` (`effect`, `baseline_comparison`, `within_arm`, `interaction`, `trend`,
  `heterogeneity`) for p-values, so a p for interaction is never read as
  the p of the effect next to it.
* `binding`: where the arm, comparator and outcome came from. A comparison
  that the text or a column header states is used as written; without one,
  an active arm against a single control is read as active versus control
  and the binding says `comparison=control_arm_convention`.
* `source_quality`: flags for values read from OCR, low confidence OCR, or
  a table whose structure is uncertain. Such values go to the review queue.
* `inputs`, `formula` and `assumptions` on derived values, and
  `supersedes` when a new derivation replaces an older one.

## Study design and methods

```{r}
r <- x$records
r[r$field %in% c("study_design", "design_features", "randomized_n", "analyzed_n", "arms", "dose",
                 "arm_n", "allocation_ratio", "follow_up", "analysis_population",
                 "primary_outcome", "secondary_outcomes"),
  c("field", "value", "arm", "method")]
```

Two `arm_n` rows per arm appear: one from the allocation sentence, one
from the column header of Table 1. The second carries a note, because a
column header does not say whether its n is the number randomized or the
number analyzed.

## Numerical results and binding

Each number is its own record. Numbers that belong together (an estimate
with its confidence limits and p-value, events with their denominator, a
mean with its dispersion) share an `observation_id`.

```{r}
o <- sc_observations(x)
o[o$observation_id == o$observation_id[o$statistic == "estimate"][1],
  c("observation_id", "statistic", "value", "outcome", "arm", "comparator", "effect_measure")]
```

The context of each number comes only from explicit structure in the
source: the subject of the sentence, a "for <outcome>" phrase after the
measure, the arm named in "in the Drug A group", a table row label, a
column header, a time point or analysis population in the table caption.
A restriction stated with the value ("among patients with diabetes", "in
the subgroup of current smokers") goes into `population`; results with
different populations are never compared with each other. The `binding`
column records which of these was used:

```{r}
unique(o$binding[o$field == "result"])
```

When the context cannot be bound, it stays `NA`; the validator then flags
the estimate (`estimate_bound`) for review instead of guessing.

The wide view puts one observation per row:

```{r}
w <- sc_observations(x, wide = TRUE)
w[w$field == "result", c("outcome", "arm", "comparator", "timepoint", "analysis_set",
                         "effect_measure", "events", "denominator", "percent",
                         "estimate", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value", "mean", "se")]
```

Text and table report the primary outcome twice: in the text without a
time point, in Table 2 at 12 months in the intention-to-treat population.
They are separate observations; the validator compares them and reports
that they agree. Each estimate takes the time point and analysis set of
its own clause; when a sentence names several and the clause does not
settle which one applies, the field stays `NA` with binding `ambiguous`.

## Ambiguity is explicit

```{r}
o[o$status %in% c("ambiguous", "missing", "not_reported"), c("statistic", "value", "status", "outcome", "arm")]
x$records$notes[x$records$status == "ambiguous"][1]
```

"8.1 &plusmn; 13.2" with no statement of SD or SE is recorded as a mean and a
`dispersion` with status `ambiguous`. A reviewer can resolve it with
`sc_correct()` once the methods section is checked.

## Evidence

```{r}
ev <- sc_evidence(x)
ev[ev$field == "result", c("record_id", "value", "page", "table_id", "cell_id", "char_start", "char_end", "bbox_scope")][1:6, ]
```

For text, the box is the union of the word boxes of the value
(`bbox_scope = "span"`); for tables, the box of the cell. The evidence
also carries the document checksum, so it can be checked against the file
later. `sc_highlight()` draws the boxes on the rendered page:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("png", quietly = TRUE)}
files <- sc_highlight(doc, x, dir = tempdir(), dpi = 60)
basename(files)
```

## Your own schema

User fields are found with a regular expression (one capture group) or a
controlled vocabulary, optionally limited to some sections:

```{r}
reg <- sc_schema("registration", fields = list(
  sc_field("ratio", "Allocation ratio", pattern = "([0-9]+:[0-9]+) ratio", sections = "methods"),
  sc_field("masking", "Masking", type = "categorical",
           vocabulary = c(double = "double-blind", single = "single-blind", open = "open-label")),
  sc_field("registry_id", "Trial registration number", pattern = "\\b(NCT[0-9]{8})\\b", required = TRUE)
))
y <- sc_extract(doc, reg)
y$records[, c("field", "value", "status", "notes")]
```

The registration number is required and absent, so it is recorded as
`not_reported` rather than left out.
